name: Clean eating

lead: Clean eating is an umbrella term for diets built around whole, minimally processed foods and avoiding refined sugar, additives and convenience products. It began in 1990s bodybuilding, where it meant high-protein, low-carbohydrate meals such as chicken, rice and vegetables, and later spread through wellness books and social media.

In looksmaxxing communities it is discussed as a baseline for leanness, skin and hormones. Researchers have described the scientific literature on clean eating as thin, with most studies looking at how people define it and how it relates to body image and eating behaviour.

paras: Practitioners favour whole foods, simple ingredient lists and less added sugar, sometimes with extra exclusions such as gluten or dairy. Forum users link this to lower insulin spikes, steadier hormones and fewer acne flares; these mechanisms are discussed in the community and have not been tested as a package.

Surveys and qualitative studies have linked rigid clean-eating beliefs with restrained eating and with orthorexia nervosa, a proposed (not formally recognised) eating disorder. Versions that cut out whole food groups have been criticised by commentators for possible nutrient gaps. Analyses of clean-eating blog recipes found nutrient profiles broadly similar to other recipes.

lead: Clean eating is an umbrella term for diets based on the belief that whole, unrefined foods bring health benefits and that processed or convenience foods should be avoided; some versions also exclude gluten, grains or dairy [1][2]. The term is described as emerging in 1990s bodybuilding, where it meant high-protein, low-carbohydrate eating that avoided sugar and junk food in order to build lean muscle, and as broadening in the 2000s through a series of "Eat-Clean" books by Tosca Reno and later wellness bloggers and influencers [2].

In looksmaxxing forums the phrase often stands for a plain staple of lean meat, rice and vegetables, and is discussed in connection with body composition, skin and hormone levels [3]. Proponents treat it as a foundation for appearance; the wider wiki entries on diet and skin cover specific foods.

Published research is limited. Wikipedia notes that there is limited research on the health effects of clean eating and that its popularity grew largely through media and anecdote [2]. Studies that do exist mostly examine how people define clean eating, its social media presence, and its associations with disordered eating [4][5][6][7][8].
infobox: Tosca Reno's Eat-Clean books (2000s); wellness bloggers and Instagram
Whole, minimally processed foods; limited refined sugar and additives

paras: There is no single agreed definition. Grokipedia describes the core as whole foods in their natural form, with fresh fruit and vegetables, lean proteins, whole grains and healthy fats, and with refined sugars, artificial additives and preservatives avoided or limited [1]. Reading ingredient labels and preferring short ingredient lists are commonly described habits [1].

A study asking US undergraduates to define clean eating found that people described it in varied ways, and examined how those perceptions related to disordered-eating indicators [4]. Because definitions differ, researchers treat it as a loose cluster of beliefs rather than one protocol [2][4].

Wikipedia traces the term to 1990s bodybuilding, where it described a lean-muscle diet avoiding sugar, fat and junk food, and credits Tosca Reno's Eat-Clean books of the 2000s with broadening it into general healthy eating [2]. Grokipedia gives an earlier 1980s bodybuilding origin and also names Reno's 2007 book and Ella Mills' Deliciously Ella (2015); the two sources differ on the decade [1].

Spread occurred through blogs, television, magazines and then Instagram hashtags such as #eatclean, often promoted by wellness figures whose advice rests largely on personal experience [1][2]. Analyses of Instagram and TikTok content have examined how clean-eating and "what I eat in a day" posts present food [9][10].
No clinical trials testing a defined clean-eating diet against a comparison diet for skin or appearance outcomes were found. The available research is observational, survey-based or qualitative.

A cross-sectional analysis of Australian women examined dietary intake, restrained eating and opinions about clean eating [8]. A comparison of nutrient composition found that recipes from popular clean-eating blogs were assessed against recipes without clean-eating claims [7]. A survey of Instagram users studied body image and health behaviours among women engaging with fitspiration and clean-eating imagery [6]. A systematic review examined eating-related social media content and its relationship with body image and eating behaviours [5].

Orthorexia nervosa, a proposed eating disorder describing an obsession with healthy or "clean" eating, is not in the DSM-5 or ICD-11; the term was introduced by physician Steven Bratman in 1997 [11]. Bratman has stressed that following a dietary theory is not orthorexia in itself, and that the term applies only when an eating disorder develops around it [11].

A study of undergraduates examining perceptions of #cleaneating reported associations with indicators of disordered eating [4]. Qualitative work with people showing orthorexic tendencies and an analysis of blogs by women who identified as having orthorexia described rigid rules and distress, and a new orthorexia measurement tool, the ONI, was developed using an online sample that included people searching for "clean eating" terms [3][12][13]. These studies describe associations and experiences, and do not establish that clean eating causes eating disorders.

Commentators generally regard the basic idea of eating more whole foods and vegetables and fewer sugary processed foods as sensible, while criticising extreme versions that remove whole food groups for lacking scientific support; one raised concern is lower calcium intake if dairy is avoided [2]. Grokipedia also notes that marketing labels claiming products are "clean" can mislead and that restrictive versions may bring nutrient deficiencies [1].

The chicken, rice and broccoli staple is a recurring reference point in bodybuilding-derived parts of looksmaxxing culture. In one looksmax.org thread, a user asked whether a long-term "clean" diet could change acne through insulin, SHBG and testosterone pathways, and another user in the thread argued that very clean eating might make the body more sensitive to insulin and androgen surges; the thread's author conceded that many other variables, such as sebum composition and the gut microbiome, were involved [3].

lore.intro: Clean eating is discussed in looksmaxxing spaces as a foundation habit for leanness and skin, often alongside bodybuilding-style meal prep [3].
